title: Standard Precautions and Transmission-Based Isolation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Use Standard Precautions for every patient, then add contact, droplet, or airborne precautions based on the suspected or confirmed pathogen. Choose PPE from the anticipated exposure, not from habit.
recognize: Blood, body fluids, nonintact skin, mucous membranes, contaminated equipment, and respiratory secretions may transmit infection.
Airborne isolation requires a fit-tested respirator and an airborne infection isolation room when available.
Contact precautions commonly require gown and gloves on room entry when contact with the patient or environment is anticipated.
priorities: Perform hand hygiene at the correct moments.
Select and don PPE before exposure.
Remove contaminated PPE without self-contamination and perform hand hygiene again.
Escalate immediately after an unprotected high-risk exposure or sharps injury.
assessMonitor: Assess the type of infectious risk and likely route of transmission.
Check isolation signage and facility policy.
Monitor for PPE breaches and contamination of shared equipment.
interventions: Use dedicated or disinfected equipment for isolation patients.
Place masks on coughing patients during transport when indicated.
Limit transport to medically necessary purposes for patients on transmission-based precautions.
redFlags: Blood or body-fluid exposure to mucosa or nonintact skin
Suspected airborne disease without appropriate respiratory protection
teaching: Teach patients and visitors why precautions are used and how to perform hand hygiene.
Explain respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette.
delegationScope: The PN follows infection-control precautions and reinforces teaching.
Do not delegate assessment of a new exposure or infection-control breach to unlicensed personnel; report and escalate per policy.
examTrap: Using the same PPE sequence for every diagnosis or assuming gloves replace hand hygiene.
oneLinePearl: Standard for everyone; add transmission precautions for the route.

title: Fall Prevention and Post-Fall Priorities
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Prevent falls by matching interventions to the patient's actual risk factors. After a fall, assess for injury and change in condition before moving the patient unless immediate danger requires movement.
recognize: High-risk clues include prior falls, gait instability, delirium, orthostasis, sedating medications, urgent toileting needs, and unfamiliar environment.
A new fall may signal acute illness, hypoglycemia, arrhythmia, bleeding, stroke, or medication effect.
priorities: Keep frequently used items and call light within reach.
Assist with transfers and toileting based on mobility level.
After a fall, assess airway, breathing, circulation, pain, neurologic status, deformity, bleeding, and vital signs before routine repositioning.
assessMonitor: Trend mental status, orthostatic symptoms, gait, medication effects, continence needs, and footwear.
Reassess after medication changes or a fall.
interventions: Use low bed position, clear pathways, adequate lighting, nonskid footwear, and appropriate assistive devices.
Use alarms only as part of an individualized plan; they do not replace observation and assistance.
medicationSafety: Review sedatives, opioids, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, and other medications that may increase fall risk; report concerning effects.
complications: Fear of falling and functional decline
redFlags: Deformity or inability to bear weight
teaching: Teach slow position changes and use of prescribed assistive devices.
Encourage asking for help before ambulation when instructed.
delegationScope: Routine ambulation assistance may be delegated when the patient is stable and the task is within policy.
A new fall or new instability requires licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Putting every high-risk patient in restraints instead of reducing modifiable risk factors.
oneLinePearl: A fall is an event and a symptom—look for the cause before resuming routine care.

title: Restraints: Least Restrictive and Time Limited
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Restraints are a last resort for immediate safety, never for convenience, punishment, or routine fall prevention. Use the least restrictive option, follow the order and monitoring requirements, and discontinue as soon as safely possible.
recognize: Agitation may come from pain, hypoxia, urinary retention, withdrawal, delirium, fear, or unmet needs.
Restraints can worsen agitation and increase injury, immobility, pressure injury, and aspiration risk.
priorities: Identify and treat reversible causes of unsafe behavior.
Attempt less restrictive measures first when feasible.
If restraints are required, protect airway, circulation, skin, alignment, hydration, elimination, and dignity.
assessMonitor: Monitor circulation, skin, behavior, respiratory status, hydration, elimination, range of motion, and ongoing need at required intervals.
Reassess after alternatives or de-escalation measures.
interventions: Use the correct device and secure it according to policy so rapid release is possible.
Provide scheduled release, mobility, toileting, nutrition, hydration, and skin care per policy and clinical condition.
medicationSafety: Do not use sedating medication solely as a chemical restraint without a legitimate clinical indication and required oversight.
redFlags: Loss of pulse or severe swelling distal to restraint
teaching: Explain the safety reason, alternatives attempted, and what must improve for discontinuation.
delegationScope: Unlicensed personnel may assist with observation and comfort measures when policy permits, but the licensed nurse remains responsible for assessment and ongoing need.
State and facility requirements vary; follow current policy.
examTrap: Applying restraints because a patient is confused and at risk for falls before trying safer alternatives.
oneLinePearl: Treat the cause, use the least restraint, reassess constantly.

title: Pressure Injury Prevention and Early Recognition
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pressure injuries are prevented by reducing pressure, shear, friction, moisture, and nutritional risk. Nonblanchable erythema on intact skin is already tissue injury and should not be massaged.
recognize: Risk rises with immobility, poor perfusion, moisture, incontinence, malnutrition, sensory loss, and medical devices.
Darkly pigmented skin may show persistent discoloration, temperature change, induration, edema, or pain before obvious color change.
priorities: Offload pressure from vulnerable areas.
Reposition based on patient condition, support surface, and tissue tolerance.
Keep skin clean and protected from excess moisture.
Report new nonblanchable discoloration or tissue breakdown promptly.
assessMonitor: Inspect bony prominences and under medical devices.
Trend nutrition, mobility, perfusion, incontinence, and skin changes.
interventions: Use pressure-redistributing surfaces and heel offloading as indicated.
Avoid donut-shaped devices and vigorous massage over reddened bony prominences.
Use lift devices to reduce shear during repositioning.
teaching: Teach weight shifting, skin inspection, nutrition, hydration, and device-related pressure prevention.
delegationScope: Routine repositioning and hygiene can be delegated for stable patients with clear instructions.
The licensed nurse assesses new skin changes and updates the care plan.
examTrap: Massaging a persistently red bony prominence to improve circulation.
sourceBasis: National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel Prevention Guidance

title: Hypoglycemia: Recognize and Treat Fast
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Treat symptomatic or confirmed hypoglycemia immediately. If the patient is awake and can swallow safely, give fast-acting carbohydrate; if unable to swallow or severely impaired, use the emergency treatment ordered/available and escalate.
recognize: Adrenergic signs include sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, and anxiety.
Neuroglycopenic signs include confusion, weakness, behavior change, seizure, and loss of consciousness.
Older adults and patients taking beta blockers may have muted warning symptoms.
priorities: Check glucose immediately when feasible without delaying treatment of a severely symptomatic patient.
Give fast-acting carbohydrate if safe to swallow.
Recheck glucose after treatment and repeat per protocol until corrected.
Escalate severe, recurrent, or unexplained hypoglycemia.
assessMonitor: Assess level of consciousness, swallow safety, recent insulin or medication timing, food intake, exercise, renal function, and alcohol use.
Trend glucose after treatment and before resuming routine insulin administration.
interventions: After recovery, provide a longer-acting carbohydrate/protein source when appropriate if the next meal is not imminent.
Identify and correct the precipitating cause before routine discharge or medication continuation.
medicationSafety: Insulin and sulfonylureas can cause significant hypoglycemia.
Do not give oral intake to a patient with impaired consciousness or unsafe swallowing.
Emergency glucagon may be used when IV access is unavailable according to orders/protocol.
redFlags: Recurrent episodes after long-acting insulin or sulfonylurea
teaching: Teach recognition, carrying rapid glucose, meal timing, medication timing, and when to seek help.
Reinforce sick-day and driving safety instructions as ordered.
delegationScope: Routine glucose checks may be delegated where policy allows, but symptomatic changes require prompt licensed-nurse evaluation.
The PN reports recurrent or severe hypoglycemia and follows emergency protocol.
examTrap: Giving juice to an unconscious patient because the glucose is low.
oneLinePearl: Low glucose plus unsafe swallow means no oral rescue.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes

title: Insulin Administration Safety
bottomLine: Insulin is a high-alert medication. Match the insulin type, dose, timing, glucose value, nutrition plan, and route before administration, then monitor for hypoglycemia and potassium shifts when clinically relevant.
recognize: Rapid-acting insulin has the greatest immediate mismatch risk when food is delayed or absent.
Basal insulin is not interchangeable with mealtime insulin.
Regular insulin is the standard insulin used intravenously when IV insulin is prescribed.
priorities: Verify the medication label, concentration, dose, route, and patient-specific glucose plan.
Ensure meal availability for prandial insulin according to timing and order.
Follow independent double-check policy when required.
assessMonitor: Check current blood glucose and trends.
Assess oral intake, NPO status, vomiting, renal function, and recent hypoglycemia.
Monitor potassium during IV insulin or major metabolic treatment when ordered.
interventions: Rotate subcutaneous sites within the same anatomic region when appropriate.
Use only insulin-specific syringes/devices matched to the concentration.
Follow facility policy for mixing insulins and never mix glargine, detemir, or degludec with other insulins.
medicationSafety: Hypoglycemia is the priority adverse effect.
Insulin can shift potassium intracellularly and contribute to hypokalemia.
Do not abbreviate units as U in handwritten communication.
redFlags: Repeated glucose below target despite treatment
Unexpected NPO status after prandial insulin administration
teaching: Teach injection technique, site rotation, storage, recognition of hypoglycemia, and matching insulin to meals/activity.
delegationScope: Insulin administration authority can vary by state and setting; follow nurse practice act and facility policy.
Clinical judgment about a new hypoglycemic event is not delegated to unlicensed personnel.
examTrap: Administering rapid-acting insulin simply because it is scheduled even though the meal tray has been delayed.
oneLinePearl: With insulin, verify the food and the glucose—not just the MAR.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes

title: Opioids: Sedation and Respiratory Depression
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sedation often precedes opioid-induced respiratory depression. Assess respiratory status and level of consciousness before and after administration; escalating sedation, slow breathing, or difficult arousal requires immediate action.
recognize: Risk increases with opioid-naive status, older age, sleep apnea, renal/hepatic impairment, high doses, and concurrent sedatives.
Pinpoint pupils may occur but are not required for diagnosis.
A normal oxygen saturation on supplemental oxygen does not guarantee adequate ventilation.
priorities: Assess respiratory rate, depth, effort, sedation, and oxygenation before giving an opioid.
Hold and escalate when ordered parameters or concerning clinical findings are present.
Support airway and ventilation and administer naloxone per emergency order/protocol when indicated.
assessMonitor: Trend sedation and respiratory status after dosing and after dose increases.
Assess pain separately from sedation; do not use pain score alone to justify another dose.
interventions: Use multimodal pain strategies when ordered.
Keep emergency response and naloxone access consistent with policy for high-risk patients.
medicationSafety: Combining opioids with benzodiazepines, alcohol, gabapentinoids, or other CNS depressants increases respiratory-depression risk.
Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, so recurrent respiratory depression can occur.
redFlags: Markedly reduced respiratory rate or shallow respirations
teaching: Teach avoidance of alcohol and unapproved sedatives, safe storage, constipation prevention, and overdose response when appropriate.
delegationScope: Pain observation may be reported by assistive personnel, but opioid administration and assessment of sedation/respiratory compromise require licensed-nurse judgment within scope.
examTrap: Giving the next opioid dose because the patient still reports pain despite being increasingly difficult to arouse.
oneLinePearl: Pain does not protect a sedated patient from respiratory depression.
sourceBasis: American Society for Pain Management Nursing Monitoring Guidance

title: Anticoagulants: Bleeding Risk and Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: The priority with anticoagulants is preventing and recognizing clinically significant bleeding while maintaining indicated therapy. New bleeding, head injury, hemodynamic change, or neurologic symptoms require urgent escalation.
recognize: Concerning findings include melena, hematemesis, hematuria, persistent epistaxis, large unexplained bruising, severe headache, weakness, and falling hemoglobin.
Warfarin effect is monitored with INR; routine INR monitoring is not used to dose direct oral anticoagulants.
priorities: Check medication, dose, indication, renal function where relevant, recent bleeding, and interacting drugs.
Use bleeding precautions appropriate to the patient.
Escalate immediately after significant bleeding or head trauma.
assessMonitor: Monitor CBC/hemoglobin and renal function as ordered.
For warfarin, monitor INR to the prescribed therapeutic range and assess dietary/drug interactions.
interventions: Apply prolonged pressure after venipuncture or injections when appropriate.
Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and trauma.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs and antiplatelet drugs can increase bleeding risk.
Warfarin has many drug and diet interactions; consistency of vitamin K intake is more important than eliminating vitamin K foods.
Reversal agents differ by anticoagulant and clinical situation.
redFlags: New severe headache or neurologic deficit
teaching: Teach signs of bleeding, medication adherence, injury prevention, and informing clinicians before procedures or starting OTC drugs.
For warfarin, reinforce INR follow-up and consistent vitamin K intake.
delegationScope: Assistive personnel may report visible bleeding, but assessment and medication decisions require licensed-nurse evaluation and provider/RN collaboration.
examTrap: Telling a warfarin patient to avoid all leafy green vegetables instead of keeping vitamin K intake consistent.
oneLinePearl: Anticoagulant plus head injury equals urgent evaluation—even if the patient feels fine.
sourceBasis: American College of Cardiology Anticoagulation Guidance

title: Digoxin: Toxicity and Safe Administration
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Digoxin toxicity is more likely with renal impairment and electrolyte disturbances, especially hypokalemia. New nausea, vomiting, anorexia, bradycardia, dysrhythmia, confusion, or visual changes should prompt holding the medication per parameters and escalation.
recognize: Toxicity may present with GI symptoms before severe cardiac effects.
Older adults and patients with reduced renal function are at higher risk.
Hypokalemia can increase sensitivity to digoxin.
priorities: Assess apical pulse/rhythm and follow ordered hold parameters before administration.
Review renal function and electrolytes when available.
Report signs of toxicity or new dysrhythmia promptly.
assessMonitor: Monitor potassium, magnesium, renal function, heart rate/rhythm, and serum digoxin level when clinically indicated.
Assess for medication interactions and recent diuretic changes.
interventions: Hold the drug and notify the appropriate clinician when toxicity is suspected according to order/policy.
Severe toxicity may require digoxin immune Fab in monitored acute care.
medicationSafety: Loop and thiazide diuretics may contribute to hypokalemia and increase toxicity risk.
Amiodarone and some other drugs can raise digoxin concentrations.
teaching: Teach pulse monitoring if prescribed, consistent dosing, and reporting GI, visual, or rhythm symptoms.
delegationScope: Medication administration must remain within licensed scope and facility policy.
Do not delegate interpretation of a new irregular pulse or toxicity symptoms to unlicensed personnel.
examTrap: Giving scheduled digoxin despite a newly low apical pulse because the blood pressure is normal.
oneLinePearl: Slow pulse plus GI or visual symptoms: think digoxin toxicity.

title: Potassium Replacement: Never IV Push
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Potassium chloride is never given by IV push. IV potassium must be diluted, infused with a pump at the ordered rate, and paired with appropriate renal-function, urine-output, and cardiac monitoring based on severity and route.
recognize: Hypokalemia can cause weakness, ileus, ECG changes, and dysrhythmias.
Hyperkalemia can also cause dangerous conduction abnormalities, so replacement errors can be fatal.
priorities: Verify the potassium level, renal function, and clinical indication.
Confirm adequate urine output or clinician-approved plan before replacement when renal impairment is possible.
Use an infusion pump and approved concentration/rate.
assessMonitor: Monitor serum potassium and renal function.
Use cardiac monitoring when ordered for significant abnormalities or higher-rate replacement.
Assess IV site for pain, phlebitis, or infiltration.
interventions: Use oral replacement when appropriate and tolerated.
Follow facility limits for peripheral versus central concentrations and rates.
medicationSafety: Never administer potassium by IV push or as an undiluted direct injection.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, and kidney failure increase hyperkalemia risk.
teaching: Teach correct use of supplements and avoiding unapproved potassium-containing salt substitutes when hyperkalemia risk exists.
delegationScope: IV medication authority varies by state and LPN/LVN scope; follow nurse practice act and facility policy.
Assessment of electrolyte instability requires licensed-nurse judgment and escalation.
examTrap: Pushing IV potassium slowly through a syringe because the serum level is dangerously low.
oneLinePearl: Potassium can be urgent—but it is never IV push.
sourceBasis: FDA Potassium Chloride Injection Prescribing Information
